title: Morgan Stanley CEO Says Your Job Shouldn't Define You
description: Morgan Stanley CEO James Gorman discusses why he doesn't mind picking up his family's pizza dinner and how he separates what he calls the "trappings of office" from his personal life. He spoke to David Rubenstein for the latest episode of Bloomberg Television's "The David Rubenstein Show: Peer-to-Peer Conversations." ----------  Like this video? Subscribe to Bloomberg on YouTube: http://www.youtube.com/Bloomberg?sub_confirmation=1  Bloomberg is the First Word in business news, delivering breaking news & analysis, up-to-the-minute market data, features, profiles and more: http://www.bloomberg.com Connect with us on... Twitter: https://twitter.com/business Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/bloombergbusiness Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/bloombergbusiness/

asr.full_text: You are very low key as by wall street standards I think so you told me a story recently that you came back the other day and you went out to pick up some pizza. Now when you're the CEO of Morgan Stanley, can't you get somebody to deliver the pizza to you or how come you have to pick it up yourself? No you know I don't regard the CEO thing as defining you as a person. I think it's you know it's everybody is different but you have to be able to, once you're not CEO, for that not to materially affect how you are as a person. And a lot of people, it does. I've seen it over many years, not everybody. Our life is very simple, we keep a very, you know, balanced sort of down-home kind of life. I mean, obviously, we live well, but you can't define – the job should not define you – your job is you're CEO from a point in time, you're helping drive the vessel, and you'll get off it, and, hopefully, it does better after you're gone. Looking at the world today, if you were starting your career all over again, would you go into finance, knowing what you now know? Yep. When I was at law school i had three jobs. It's true story and one of them was I worked in a sheet metal factory melting sheet metal together, which was incredibly difficult. The second was I was the toilet cleaner at my college, which was an all mail college, which was an all-male college, which was … incredibly difficult job. And the third one is working on Saturdays at the local brokerage firm, called Potter Partners, which is now owned by a global firm, helping match trades that would not be matched during the week. So the loose-end trades. And I love the business then. The first shares I bought were oil exploration options, which is about as far on the risk, but I was- Did you make money on it? Yeah, but I was 19 years old, why not take some risk? You have no responsibility, I loved the business, I loved markets, I loved the business, and I loved working with CEOs and clients and trying to get good financial transactions done. You have children, are they in the financial markets? No, no, they are not. One ah, one is working in DC, in consulting business, and one is still in college, and she's an artist, an musician, very creative. So when you became the CEO of Morgan Stanley, did they treat you differently? They have more respect than before, or no? David Weinberg, Sr.:? Not really, no. No, we're very grounded. The kids are great and I spent a lot of time with them going through the SAT tests and visiting colleges and all that sort of stuff. And you know first and foremost, you're dad and want to be as normal a dad in most ways is almost your dad and you want to be as normal a dad as you can and and hopefully some of the trappings of office and the stuff around it. You've got to keep that away from your family. Your family is your family. So they don't say my dad is the CEO of Morgan Stanley? They don't tell people that I don't think so? No, you know they're trying to build their own lives. And you know, like all of us, we want for our kids to have the right level of independence,
